newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Pulp, paper slump hits earnings for NZ's Fletcher.
newsitem.headline: Pulp, paper slump hits earnings for NZ's Fletcher.

text.p: A slump in pulp and paper prices and a sharp spike up in oil prices combined to form a mixed bag for New Zealand conglomerate Fletcher Challenge when its four divisions reported their first half earnings on Wednesday.

Fletcher Paper, the biggest division and one with the highest exposure to commodities cycles, fell into a loss of NZ$40 million (US$27.8 million) in the six months to December, a dramatic turnaround from a NZ$186 million profit a year earlier.
On the brighter side was Fletcher Energy, with a sharp rise in earnings to NZ$126 million from $20 million.
Fletcher Forests followed up with a decline in net earnings to NZ$37 million from $48 million, which was in line with expectations.
Fletcher Building disappointed with a net profit of NZ$53 million against $77 million and compared with expectations of $65-75 million.
"Forests was in line. Paper was as expected and looking very clouded going forward," John Cairns at Cavill White Securities said. "Building is a bit disappointing and Energy looks great."
FCL Chief Executive Hugh Fletcher said it had been a year of varying fortunes for all the divisions.

"At the high end of the see-saw has been Energy and the low end Paper, whilst Building and Forests have straddled the fulcrum," Fletcher told a news conference. "The driver of these varying fortunes has been the external environment, most particularly global product prices," he said.
Cairns said Building was disappointing at an operating level, mostly due to continued low prices for medium density fibreboard (MDF).
"They are pulling a lot of costs out of the (MDF) business but going forward, the outlook is pretty negative," Cairns said.
The extent of writeoffs for Australian and U.S. construction businesses, after a sizeable provision last year, also surprised.
Paper was affected by interruptions at New Zealand and Canadian mills through maintenance and addition of new plant.

Of FCL's offshore subsidiaries, U.K. Paper ran up an operating loss of NZ$23 million owing to continuing weakness in the European fine paper markets. Strong wood products markets boosted the contribution to earnings by Canada's TimberWest to NZ$22.0 million from $7.0 million.
Compared to the half year to June 1996, newsprint fell US$160 per tonne to US$557, pulp was off US$40 a tonne to $US$559 and lightweight coated paper fell US$180 to US$797.
Energy reported a 14 percent rise in production to 23.7 million barrels of oil equivalent over the period, mostly due to the commissioning of a floating storage facility off the Taranaki coast.
The Maharaja Lela project, offshore Brunei, is scheduled to start production in January 1999.
Guy Hallwright at First NZ Capital said Energy's result was in line with expectations, even though the stock gained nine to NZ$3.92 on the back of it.
"It's very undervalued, I think, but everyone was expecting a result pretty much like this," he said.
Fletcher Challenge consolidated first half net profit fell to NZ$192 million from $360 million a year earlier.
